title: Jane speaks for herself
summary: While Jane waits to be sent away, resistance has altered her relation to the Reeds: even John retreats when she defends herself. Mrs. Reed introduces her to Mr. Brocklehurst, the severe clergyman who runs Lowood Institution. Brocklehurst uses fear of hell and a doctrine of humility to judge Jane, while Mrs. Reed brands her deceitful and asks that Lowood keep her isolated even during vacations. After he leaves, Jane directly tells Mrs. Reed that the accusation is false, that she does not love her, and that she will tell others how cruelly she was treated. Mrs. Reed retreats, making this Jane's first moral victory, though triumph gives way to remorse and loneliness. Before Jane departs, Bessie's imperfect affection provides stories, conversation, and a tender farewell.
events: Jane's new willingness to fight back deters John Reed.
Mr. Brocklehurst examines Jane through threats of damnation and promises to cultivate humiliation at Lowood.
Mrs. Reed preemptively labels Jane deceitful and arranges that she remain at school during holidays.
Jane confronts Mrs. Reed with the truth and wins temporary emotional ground.
Bessie and Jane share a gentler farewell before Jane leaves Gateshead.

characters.name: Jane Eyre
characters.development: She discovers that plain truth can defend her identity against an adult's false narrative, even though anger alone does not bring peace.

characters.name: Mrs. Reed
characters.development: Attempts to extend control beyond Gateshead by poisoning Jane's reputation at Lowood.

characters.name: Mr. Brocklehurst
characters.development: Introduced as an authority who equates poverty, fear, and humiliation with Christian education.

characters.name: Bessie
characters.development: Offers Jane the closest thing to familial tenderness available at Gateshead.

themes: Religious language used as social discipline
The exhilaration and cost of anger

threads.text: Jane is accepted for Lowood and will leave Gateshead.
Mrs. Reed's accusation of deceit may shape Jane's treatment at school.
Jane's resistance succeeds outwardly but does not yet reconcile justice, anger, and inner calm.
